newsitem.title: FRANCE: Madcow inquiry committee prepares to grill Santer.
newsitem.headline: Madcow inquiry committee prepares to grill Santer.

text.p: A probe into the handling of the mad cow crisis comes to a head this week as the European Parliament prepares to claim that Britain and the European Commission mishandled the affair.
The head of a parliamentary committee of inquiry into the mad cow epidemic said on Tuesday that Britain should be taken to court for failing to cooperate with his panel's investigation.

He vowed also to demand an explanation from Commission President Jacques Santer, who faces the committee on Wednesday, on how exactly the Commission planned to meet Parliament demands for changes in its procedures.
"It is important that the Commission should have clearly spelled out to it what conclusions it should draw," committee chairman Reimer Boege told a news conference on Tuesday.
Santer's performance on Wednesday could have a bearing on the final shape of a report which the 19-member cross-party panel is to conclude on February 6.
The report follows the committee's four-month investigation into the BSE crisis, which has ravaged British herds and scared shoppers across the continent.
A draft of the report, which the Parliament is to vote on on February 19, strongly attacks Britain and the Commission for mishandling the crisis over BSE, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy.

The report accuses the British government of negligence on 13 counts, and says that the Commission's delay in releasing data on BSE helped to undermine public confidence and worsen the economic damage.
Committee members remain divided, however, over whether to recommend specific sanctions, including legal action against Britain and a motion of censure against the Commission.
Boege said Santer would be asked to address a string of specific problems highlighted by the report.
These include the difficulty of pinning down who exactly was responsible for what went wrong and how to deal with pressure on Commission officials from national governments, in this case Britain.
"Powers are distributed in such a way that you cannot determine who is responsible," the report's author, Manuel Medina Ortega, told reporters on Tuesday.
Medina, a Spanish Socialist, recommended creation of an independent European body, free of pressure from national governments, to deal with public health issues.

European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has said the Parliament's criticisms are partially justified but Consumer Affairs Comissioner Emma Bonino said in Paris on Tuesday it was unfair of the Parliament to blame the current Commission for mistakes made by its predecessors.

Medina and Boege told Reuters they both thought the Parliament, the Commission or both should take legal action against Britain for refusing to send Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg to testify before the committee of inquiry.
The committee must decide on February 6 whether to follow this line of action, which Boege described as "explosive stuff".
Britain argues that it is under no legal obligation to send Hogg to the committee and has met the committee's needs by presenting testimony from a senior civil servant.
Boege, a German Christian Democrat, said a principle was at stake. "It is not just a case of Hogg but the future of all committees of inquiry," he said.
He acknowledged, however, that the Commission was unlikely to consider legal action before the British general election, which must be called by May 22.
